messages.subject: Re: Distance Sampling for flying seabirds
parts:
Hi Dave,

I thought it would be worth adding my 10 pence to this, having used and
thought about the snapshot method (2 in your list of questions) extensive=
ly
over the years.

One of the main reasons that there has been such strong take-up of this
method is that it still works at very high encounter rates, which I fear
would not be the case if observers are asked to collect too much informat=
ion
at the time of the snapshot.

It is key to the snapshot method that it happens over as short a time fra=
me
as possible (Tony Gaston simulated the effect of extended snapshots in a
response to the Tasker et al. publication in The Auk (1987, 104:336-338))=
.=20
This is another reason for not trying to collect too much information at =
the
time of the snapshot count.

Measuring distances accurately at sea is problematic, so I would hazard
caution against trying to do anything too precise. Also, one of the
assumptions of distance estimation is that animals are not reacting
(attracted to or repelled by) the observer or the observation base. I th=
ink
that for some species, this is a significant problem, and a complex metho=
d
for estimating their abundance is giving you false precision.=20=20

I'm interested in Steve's suggestion of using a circular snapshot area
rather than a box-shape (I think a 90deg segment would be more practical)=
.=20
I would certainly expect it to be easier for observers than a box shape. =
It
would be necessary to make adjustments to the way the snapshot method is
implemented, because the box-shaped snapshot simulates a complete strip
transect of 300 metres width for flying birds, and intervals between
snapshots are determined by the time it takes to travel the length of the=
box.=20

I'd be very interested in hearing how you get on with any trials of optio=
n 3.

Best wishes

Andy

On Mon, 21 Apr 2008 15:29:18 +0100, Steve Buckland <st...@MCS.ST-AND.AC.U=
K>
wrote:

> >Fifield,David [St. John's] wrote:
>> >> We conduct at-sea surveys for pelagic seabirds in eastern Canadian
>> >> waters. At the recent Pacific Seabird Group meeting I had the
>> >> opportunity to discuss distance sampling for flying birds with other
>> >> North American pelagic surveyors.
>> >>
>> >> A number of methods for dealing with flying birds are currently in use=
:
>> >>
>> >> 1. Count flying birds continuously, record distance at which bird was
>> >> first detected.
>> >> =09- I asked about recording distances when birds are first
>> >> detected at the Distance workshop last year. I remember the consensus
>> >> was that this wasn't a good idea, but don't remember the details. Can
>> >> someone explain why or why not?
>> >> =09- I think the continuous counting still overestimates flying
>> >> birds.
>> >>
> >Yes, it does. This is because, if birds are flying, you preferentially
> >record them when they are relatively close to the line, as they are
> >easier to detect then. Hence distances tend to be biased low, which
> >generates upward bias in the abundance estimate.
>> >> 2. Tasker's "snapshot" method, no distance sampling
>> >> =09- deals with overestimates due to continuous counting, but fails
>> >> to estimate detectability.
>> >>
> >Works fine if you can accurately assess where the box is, and can detect=

> >all birds in the box.
>> >> 3. Tasker's "snapshot method", distances recorded at moment of snapsho=
t
>> >> =09- I think this will work fine and I'm really interested to hear
>> >> arguments either for or against it.
> >This is akin to the snapshot method mentioned in the point transect
> >chapter of the 2001 book - see p147 and 173. Yes, if you can record
> >distances from the line of each bird in flight at the snapshot moment,
> >this approach is fine. It also works fine in a point transect
> >framework, where e.g. you record all visible birds in flight within a
> >sector ahead of the observer at the snapshot moment.
>> >>
>> >>
>> >> The Intro book (section 6.5.1, p. 202) recommends recording distances
>> >> when a flying bird comes abeam, regardless of when it was detected; OR=
a
>> >> slightly modified scheme (p. 203) where the "beam line" is projected
>> >> ahead of the ship, but still perpendicular to the transact. Both these=

>> >> methods require constant tracking of flying birds to detect when they
>> >> cross the beam line, no matter where it is placed. Most observers felt=

>> >> this method would divert attention away from the transect line,
>> >> resulting in loss of detections of birds on water at distance zero (i.=
e.
>> >> on the line) and it also may be quite onerous when it is busy.
>> >>
>> >> The snapshot method in no. 3 above has the advantage that flying birds=

>> >> can be ignored (if necessary during busy periods) until the moment of
>> >> the instantaneous snapshots. At which point, all birds within the
>> >> snapshot box are counted and their distances recorded. A minor
>> >> disadvantage is that the observer still has to estimate whether the
>> >> birds are inside or outside the box, which I believe is no harder than=

>> >> estimating when they cross a beam line projected ahead of the ship.
>> >>
> >Might be better to have a circular plot, if you're able to record
> >distances at the snapshot moment (possibly in distance bands). The plot=

> >is then a circle or part-circle, centre located at the observer. The
> >data would be analysed in the standard way for point transect sampling,
> >but if you have a sector with angle say 90 degrees, effort per point
> >would be 0.25 (90/360).
> >
> >Steve Buckland
>> >> So, can anyone see anything about number 3 that drastically violates t=
he
>> >> basic assumptions of Distance Sampling or suggest a better method?
>> >>
>> >> Thanks for your help,
>> >> Dave
>> >>
>> >>
